speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It empowers the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) to maintain a record of births and deaths in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This record is also important for policy-making and the provision of public services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It allows, for example, the Government to plan for the needs of our population in areas such as education and housing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This Bill will repeal and re-enact the RBDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, to mandate the reporting of every birth, death and stillbirth in Singapore as well as those on board an aircraft, vessel or train that is bound for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, to consolidate the registration of all births under the same legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fifth, to empower the Registrar-General of Births and Deaths, or RG in short, to register births, deaths and stillbirths under special circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Sixth, to empower the RG and ICA officers to investigate and enforce against offences under the RBDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, on reporting of birth, deaths and stillbirths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The current Act requires certain persons to register births, deaths and stillbirths but does not impose a mandatory reporting requirement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To be clear, reporting is different from registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The reporting of a birth, death or stillbirth is an important first step.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It alerts the relevant authorities to the occurrence of the event.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: After a birth, death or stillbirth is reported, the next step is registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the case of births, for example, the RG will register the birth after the parents or legally appointed persons have provided a name for the child and other birth particulars.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This Bill will impose a mandatory reporting requirement on persons defined in clauses 7, 22 and 32 for local births, deaths and stillbirths respectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This includes a medical practitioner who attends to a birth in a hospital and, for deaths outside a hospital, an occupier of the premises who knows of the death.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This does not include deaths reportable under the Coroners Act, such as unnatural deaths or deaths where the identity of the deceased is unknown.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such deaths will continue to be reported to the Police, as currently required under the Coroners Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill expands the scope of the RBDA to include the reporting of births, deaths and stillbirths on board an aircraft, vessel or train – henceforth referred to as a conveyance – that is outside of but bound for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 10 of the Bill makes it mandatory for births on an inbound conveyance to be reported to the RG as soon as practicable after arrival in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Likewise, clauses 26 and 35 mandate that deaths and stillbirths on an inbound conveyance be reported to the Police as soon as practicable after arrival in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The current RBDA requires a parent of a child born in Singapore or any person who is present at the birth or in charge of the child to furnish the child's birth particulars to the RG within 14 days, so that the RG can register the birth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An application for registration made after 14 days but by 42 days after the child's birth is considered a delayed registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The timeline of 42 days will provide sufficient time for the parents and legally appointed persons to provide the child's birth particulars, which include an appropriate name for the child.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An exception is made under clause 8 in the case of a child who dies within 42 days after birth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In such a case, the persons responsible for providing birth particulars are exempted from that requirement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Instead, the RG will register the birth on his own volition under clause 9 based on available particulars from the death reporting of the deceased child.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will relieve the grieving parents of the birth registration formalities during such a difficult time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, on consolidating the registration of all births under the RBDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, the birth of an adopted child is registered or reregistered under the Adoption of Children Act while the birth of a child out of wedlock is legitimated and reregistered under the Legitimacy Act if the parents subsequently register their marriage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For a child to whom the Status of Children (Assisted Reproduction Technology) Act applies or who is legitimated under that Act, his or her birth is registered or re-registered in accordance with the current RBDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 14 and 15 of the Bill will consolidate the registration of births currently in the Adoption of Children Act and the Legitimacy Act under the RBDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This consolidation will impose the same registration requirements on all local births, such as the requirements and restrictions on the name of a child under clause 19.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 16 to 18 will allow for births of children to whom the Status of Children (Assisted Reproduction Technology) Act applies, or who is legitimated under that Act to continue to be registered, or re-registered under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Accordingly, the Adoption of Children Act, Legitimacy Act and Status of Children (Assisted Reproduction Technology) Act will be amended by clauses 64, 66 and 69 respectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, two steps are needed to register a death in Singapore: (a) a medical practitioner certifies the death and issues an electronic Certificate of the Cause of Death (COD) Certificate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A printout of the certificate is then given to the deceased person’s relative; (b) the relative brings the COD Certificate to a registration centre, which are public hospitals, Neighbourhood Police Centres or Posts, or ICA, and applies for death registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In other words, the relative will no longer need to provide the death particulars at a registration centre.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As mentioned earlier, a death in Singapore, other than a reportable death under the Coroners Act, must be reported to a medical practitioner as soon as practicable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Upon receiving the report, the medical practitioner must examine the deceased person’s body as soon as practicable and ascertain relevant information regarding the circumstances of the death.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Thereafter, if the death is not a reportable death under the Coroners Act, the medical practitioner must, within 24 hours after examining the body, certify the death online by providing the cause of death and other death particulars to the RG under clause 23.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the case of a reportable death under the Coroners Act, the deceased person’s relative also does not need to register the death.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The RG will automatically register the death under clause 24 after receiving the Coroner’s certificate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fifth, on enhancing the powers of the RG to register births, deaths and stillbirths under special circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I will cover the various special circumstances in turn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 9 empowers the RG to register a birth in Singapore on his own volition in the absence of complete birth particulars.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This additional power is important for the welfare of children born in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It ensures that every child is given a legal identity and his or her presence is made known to other Government agencies, to allow for Government intervention or support if necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The RG will exercise this power if the responsible persons for a child fail to furnish the birth particulars for birth registration, and where attempts to contact the responsible persons are futile.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In registering such a birth, the RG will give the child an appropriate name.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 20 provides that a responsible person may apply to the RG to change the name given by the RG within seven years after the child’s birth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A second scenario is a local death where the deceased person’s body is destroyed, not recoverable or cannot be located.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In these circumstances, currently, the deceased person’s family will need to wait for the issuance of a Coroner’s certificate before an application for death registration can be made.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will allow the deceased person’s family to proceed with post-death matters in a more timely manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To determine that such a death has occurred in the absence of a body, the RG will rely on information and evidence from competent authorities, such as the Police and the Singapore Civil Defence Force, and any other relevant persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If the RG is not satisfied that the death has occurred or cannot confirm the identity of the deceased person, he will not register the death.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The deceased person’s family will then need to wait for the outcome of the Coroner’s Inquiry and the issuance of the Coroner’s certificate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For clarity, this provision does not apply to missing persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The next-of-kin of a missing person who wishes to have the missing person presumed by law to be dead will need to apply to the Court for the necessary order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A third scenario is births, deaths and stillbirths on board a conveyance that is outside of, but bound for, Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As mentioned earlier, clauses 10, 26 and 35 of the Bill impose a mandatory reporting requirement for such events.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, registration is not mandatory as the births, deaths and stillbirths did not happen in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The parents of a child or a stillborn child, and the relatives of a deceased person, can choose whether to register the event in Singapore, or only when they return to their home country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 13, 27 and 36 will allow the RG to register such births, deaths and stillbirths, if the parents or relatives choose to and make an application to register the event in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This expanded scope of the RG’s powers will provide administrative ease in cases where a child, or a deceased person’s body, arrives in Singapore, and official documentation is needed by the receiving country to which the parents or relatives wish to bring the child or body.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It also caters for instances where the home country of the child’s parents or the deceased person is not able to register the birth, death or stillbirth under its laws.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under clause 28, the RG may register the death of a Singapore Citizen or Permanent Resident, or PR, who dies overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is provided that the deceased person’s body is brought back to Singapore and the death is not registered overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The relative of the deceased person must make an application within three months after the death and provide a medical document certifying the cause of death.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This expanded scope will cater to the registration of overseas deaths of Singaporeans and PRs that are not able to be registered overseas for some reason.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This may include, for example, the temporary closure of government services overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The requirement for the body to be brought back to Singapore is to prevent fraudulent registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Hence, this power does not extend to an overseas death where the body is not found.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In such a case, the relative of the deceased person will need to apply to the Court for an order on the presumption of death, if the death is not registered with the foreign authorities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Last but not least, the powers of the RG and ICA officers will be enhanced to facilitate investigation and enforcement against offences under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under clause 42, the RG will be empowered to obtain information required to perform his functions as well as ascertain whether a registrable event has occurred or whether a provision in the Act has been complied with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The RG will also be empowered under clause 44 to take possession of false or invalid documents produced in connection with the reporting and registration of births, deaths and stillbirths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under clauses 45 and 46, ICA officers who are appointed as authorised registration officers will be able to conduct searches and investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A woman gives birth to a child in a hospital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The attending medical practitioner files a Notification of Live Birth to report the birth to the RG; the parents do not need to do this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Anytime within 42 days after the birth, the parents must register the birth either online using the LifeSG mobile application or in person at ICA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Once this is done, the parents will receive a notification to download the digital birth certificate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The relatives may then download the digital death certificate from the My Legacy website.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For deaths that occur at home, a relative who is present must report the death to a medical practitioner, who will conduct a home visit to examine the body and certify the cause of death online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: When a woman gives birth to a stillborn child in a hospital, a medical practitioner will examine the body and certify the cause of death online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The stillbirth particulars are then conveyed electronically to the RG, who will automatically register the stillbirth; the parents no longer need to do this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The parents may then download the digital stillbirth certificate from the My Legacy website.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Second Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These amendments, Madam, will significantly increase convenience for the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is important because the reporting and registration of births and deaths is not just a bureaucratic process of record-keeping.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the registration of a birth and death can have far-reaching legal and social implications for the individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points to make on the registration of births.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on births with insufficient particulars.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 9(3), the Registrar-General may also register a birth without a name for the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In such cases, a responsible person for the child must apply to register a name of the child within seven years of the birth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, seven years is a very long time for a child not to have a registered name.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Registrar-General has broad powers to obtain information under the new section 42(1).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the Bill places obligations on responsible persons for the registration of births, can the Minister clarify whether the Registrar-General or ICA will take a proactive approach in following up with the responsible persons in such cases of incomplete particulars or missing names?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Taking a proactive approach where the responsible persons are unable or unwilling to meet their obligations is important as proper registration may have implications on the child who does not have any power over the registration process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the support to children who are stateless by being born in Singapore to non-citizen parents who did not or could not obtain citizenship for their children from their home countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Of this number, about three-quarters are Singapore Permanent Residents, or PRs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that ICA evaluates every application for PR or citizenship on a range of criteria and the applicant's circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if ICA informs other Ministries, in particular, MSF, of children registered at birth as stateless to ensure that these children do not fall through the gaps in social and educational support?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that citizenship has to be granted based on careful assessment of a range of factors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also appreciate that some degree of social and educational support is already extended to stateless children with PR status.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, stateless children and their families have to jump through additional bureaucratic hoops in order to obtain social and educational support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even where citizenship cannot be immediately granted, can the ICA work together with other Ministries to make it easier for stateless children to obtain the necessary support, or even to proactively reach out to this group of who may be more vulnerable without the guarantees and protections of citizenship?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about children born to single unwed mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are children who do not have a father named on their birth certificate or who have a father named on the birth certificate who is not married to the mother.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, ECDA works with the Social Service Offices, Family Service Centres and hospitals to reach out to pregnant mothers and families who can benefit from KidSTART.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand from some single unwed mothers that social workers have approached mothers at the hospital to provide support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if there is a system of informing MSF of all children who are, again, born to single unwed mothers, whether in hospitals or otherwise, so that MSF can look into extending the necessary support to these families?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It provides clear rules on who holds the responsibility to report to the Government in the event of birth or death under a wide range of foreseeable scenarios.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While I support the Bill, I have a few clarifications to seek.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the current Registration of Births and Deaths Act, section 10 provides guidance on how a child's surname is given although there is no explicit reference to double-barrelled surnames.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Currently, parents are able to register their child with a double-barrelled surname if they choose to do so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, under the Bill, there is no longer any reference to surname.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister give us some guidance to the kinds of surnames that would be permissible for the child?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a parent of children of mixed ethnicity myself, I am particularly conscious of this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2011, ICA implemented the registration of double-barrelled race options for Singaporean children born to parents of different ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By this new option, if one parent is Chinese and the other is Indian, the child's race may be recorded as Chinese, or Indian, or Chinese-Indian, or Indian-Chinese, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this respect, I wonder if the Registry of Births and Deaths is able to provide some indication of trends, in similar fashion to what is reported on marriages, on the proportion of births to parents of different ethnicities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I also wonder if the Ministry would consider streamlining the process by which parents of mixed ethnicity can apply to change the racial classification on their child's NRIC to a double-barrelled racial classification in cases where the child was registered at birth as bearing solely one ethnicity as they would have had to be prior to 2011.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, it would appear that both parents need to visit ICA for a physical interview in order to effect this change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could the parents be enabled to provide their consent digitally or via a virtual meeting, for example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, the Chinese-Indian example given by ICA in their website falls within the Chinese, Malay, Indian and Others (CMIO) framework.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is it also possible to assign double-barrelled race classifications to a child in Singapore that is outside the CMIO framework, for example, Chinese-Burmese or Korean-Vietnamese?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Like surnames, there appear to be no explicit rules in respect of designation of race of the child in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, ICA states in their website that it currently includes the option for parents to include ethnic characters of the child's name in Chinese, Jawi or Tamil.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given the increasing ethnic diversity in our demographic make-up, will the ICA also be open to requests for other ethnic characters as well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, if the child is of mixed ethnicity, will they also be given the option to have their name spelled out in two sets of ethnic characters?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that obtaining the death certificate is essential for identification and authentication purposes before some funeral services can be provided for the deceased.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At present, the next-of-kin would have to express the preferred mode of disposal, cremation or burial when they register the death.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The next-of-kin would then receive a permit to bury or cremate contained in the death certificate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Based on that, a funeral director would then be able to proceed to book slots for cremation or burial.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A death certificate may also be required to engage your funeral director in order for services, such as the embalming of bodies and the use of funeral parlour compounds, to be performed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On a separate but not unrelated note, I would like to ask if funeral service providers were consulted in the course of formulating this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I would like to clarify how relatives, who are not digitally-savvy, would be able to receive the death certificate once it has issued.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Relatives need this death certificate in order to commence funeral preparations and in their state of grief, they may be anxious to obtain it as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that the new system allows for the process to be performed online and a digital notification will be sent to the relative to download the digital death certificate from the Government's online portal when it is ready.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, there may be cases – admittedly, perhaps, not too many – when none of the relatives of the deceased who are planning the funeral are IT literate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would provisions be made in such cases to enable the relatives to collect a physical copy of the death certificate at a location that is nearby?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, the Bill highlights that the family should destroy the identification card to prevent abuse.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the Registration of Births and Deaths Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Simplifying the registration process and digitalising it will bring more convenience to our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to become a Smart City, it is necessary to digitalise the births and deaths registration process.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will strengthen Government agencies' capability in identification and verification to provide better services for the people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The latest technologies, such as blockchain, can prevent theft and hacking, ensuring that electronic data be stored permanently and securely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, I hope that the Government will consider adding an extra layer of protection to our registration records through different data retention methods.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the new regulation proposed by the Ministry to make it mandatory for persons responsible to report births and deaths to the authorities, doctors or the Police as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Being born in our country does not mean that the babies will automatically acquire citizenship.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So far, how many newborns are not registered or abandoned by their parents each year?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does our country have institutions or facilities to accept abandoned babies?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These records assist in ensuring that our population data is accurate and allows us to use this information to plan and enact policies to respond to the needs of our population.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I wish to seek some clarifications from the Minister of State for Home Affairs on certain provisions of this Bill in four areas.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, the present Bill seeks to streamline and digitise the death registration process.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The new process requires a medical practitioner to certify and submit the death of a person online following which the death certificate is issued digitally.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I also understand that the doctor or hospital can assist in printing the certificate for families who have difficulties accessing the digital certificates.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister of State clarify if this new process will result in increased fees compared to the current process since, for example, the doctor will now have to print the certificate or is it envisaged for it to be without charge?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Two, I also note that according to the Second Schedule in the current Registration of Births and Deaths Rules, there is a listing of fees such as persons are required to pay a $40 fee for certified extract of birth or death from the register in Forms L and M respectively.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The body was not brought back to Singapore and he, therefore, is unable to bring closure to their estate matters after many years.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   This Bill will enable doctors to certify and manage the registration of deaths online without requiring the relative of the deceased person to register at the hospital, police station or ICA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will help to simplify and expedite the funeral arrangements process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The process of funeral arrangements and burial is an important one for Muslims.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a collective religious obligation of Muslims and it is a priority for our community to complete this process without delay, so that the burial can take place as soon as practicable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Pusara Aman Mosque near the Pusara Aman Cemetery, which is also located within the Keat Hong ward in Chua Chu Kang, is one of several mosques that actively serve Muslims in our country by providing facilities for funeral arrangements before burial takes place at the Pusara Aman Cemetery.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, during the COVID-19 pandemic and the previous circuit breaker period, our mosques like the Pusara Aman Mosque are also busy serving those in our community whose family members have passed away.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During my visits, I was informed that the mosques also saw an increase in funeral arrangements done within the mosque compound as compared to last time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With Singapore’s ageing population, this may increase in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The implementation of digital technology put forth in this Bill will help to reduce the likelihood of mistakes in the death registration process that may be caused by human error.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was informed about a case last year that happened at the Pusara Aman Mosque.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the hustle and bustle of funeral arrangements, an error occurred in one of the death registrations, where the signature and reference number columns were not filled in by the agency and the family of the deceased person.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Due to that, the burial could not proceed on the same day until the certificate was corrected.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Police and family of the deceased person eventually re-registered the death and obtained a new certificate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, by the time the process was completed, it was too late in the day and the burial could only take place the next day.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I welcome the provisions in this Bill that will help to expedite and facilitate the death registration process in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With this, I hope that it will also mitigate the risk of errors occurring during registration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also support the provisions that require all deaths in Singapore to be reported as soon as practicable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Notwithstanding my support for the Bill, I would like to seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the registration of deaths, I have four clarifications.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would there be any safeguards against extra charges or costs to be borne since doctors are now not only certifying deaths, but they are also helping to submit the certification online?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would it be useful for ICA to still retain some powers to investigate non-reporting offences in cases where there are more than one responsible person who can report?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, take the case if person A could have made the report earlier in time but deliberately did not do so and, subsequently, person B reported the death.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By section 22(4), person A would have been absolved from liability, notwithstanding that his deliberate omission goes against the mandatory requirement of reporting "as soon as practicable after the death" and the intent of the Bill to promote expeditious reporting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, all hospital births, or children brought to the hospital within 24 hours of being born, are reported but it is not mandatory for births outside of hospitals to be reported to the authorities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now, almost anyone, including parents or a proxy on behalf of the parents, can provide the child's birth particulars to ICA for registration within 42 days from the date of birth.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For reporting of births in any other places, the responsibility falls squarely on the parents only.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, for reporting of deaths in any other places, the responsibility falls on, inter alia, every relative of the deceased person who knows of the death.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MHA also consider placing the obligation of reporting of birth on a relative of the parents who knows or have knowledge of such birth?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be useful in situations where the parents themselves breach such registration requirements and where the birth did not occur in the premises which are occupied by relatives.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My last clarification is a general one on ICA's own resourcing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under the new rules, ICA officers would take over investigation of offences relating to the registration of births and deaths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would ICA be forming a new department in this regard?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To summarise, this Bill will bring about three key benefits: first, the Bill will provide greater convenience to Singaporeans through streamlined registration processes; second, the Bill will cater for an expanded scope of registration scenarios; third, the Bill will strengthen ICA's enforcement powers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Please allow me to address the questions from the Members in turn.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim said that the new digitalised process would reduce errors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked whether we will still keep a hard copy of the registration records in case the electronic system fails and the data is lost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While ICA will not be keeping hard copy records for registrations done digitally, measures are taken to ensure that the data of the digital records are backed up at alternate secured sites and retrievable in the event of system failures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr Derrick Goh asked whether there will be any extra charges or costs to be borne.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While the Government is not able to dictate the fees charged by private hospitals and general practitioners who make house visits to certify deaths, we note that private hospitals and general practitioners will continue to use the same ICA e-service, which they are already using currently to certify deaths online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Hence, we do not expect the costs incurred by the private hospitals and general practitioners to increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked if fees would be imposed for extracts from the registers, given that they will be issued digitally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Regardless of the format of the extract, there is still a need to recover the costs for providing this service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If the costs have come down, the fees will be revised accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim raised questions regarding the categories of responsible persons and their duties to report births and deaths under the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Under clause 7, where a birth occurs in any premises other than in a hospital, the child's parents and the occupier of the premises who knows of the birth in the premises are responsible for the reporting of the birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Under the Bill, an occupier for any premises includes a person who has control of, or is managing, the premises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, the management of a mall who knows of a birth in the mall, or the owner of an apartment who knows of a birth in the apartment, will be responsible for reporting the birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In most cases, we would expect the parents to be responsible for reporting the birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Under clause 22, where a death occurs in any premises other than in a hospital, the relative of the deceased person who is present at the death, and the occupier of the premises who knows of the death in the premises, are responsible for reporting the death.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In most cases, we would expect the relatives to be responsible for reporting the death.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim highlighted that for births that occur in a place other than hospitals, premises and conveyances, the responsibility falls squarely on the parents only.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, for the reporting of deaths in any other place, the responsibility falls on, inter alia, every relative of the deceased person who knows of the death.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He asked for MHA's rationale for this difference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He also asked whether the relatives of a child should also be included as responsible persons who should report the child's birth under clause 7(2).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The situations surrounding births and deaths are different.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For a newborn child, the parents are the responsible persons who will need to care for the child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Hence, they are legally required to report the birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Under the current Act, ICA occasionally encounters birth registrations by persons other than the parents, such as a relative of the child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While ICA will continue to accept reports of births from relatives who are aware of the births, we do not want to burden the relatives with the legal obligation to report or be penalised for failing to report the birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For a deceased person passing away in any other place, the circumstances of death and the persons who may know of the death may be vastly different for each case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: A deceased person could have died alone or in the company of a relative or a non-related person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Hence, the provision under clause 22(2)(d) provides for a wider scope of responsible persons than that for births under clause 7(2)(e).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As for the scenario mentioned by Mr Derrick Goh of a jogger who finds a dead body, the death will fall under the purview of the Coroners Act as a reportable death since it is likely that the death occurred under suspicious circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For a reportable death, the jogger is obligated under section 5 of the Coroners Act to report it to a Police officer as soon as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As the death is not under the scope of clause 22 of the Bill, the jogger does not need to report the death to a medical practitioner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked if it would be useful for ICA to still retain some powers to investigate non-reporting offences in cases where there are multiple responsible persons who can report.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Under clause 22(4), as long as a responsible person reports a death, the duty of every other responsible person is discharged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is because once a report has been made and a medical practitioner is alerted to the death, the purpose of the reporting requirement is met.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, if no responsible person reports the death, all responsible persons, who do not have a reasonable excuse, shall be guilty of the offence of failing to report the death.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This provides sufficient deterrence against the failure to report a death while achieving the aim of ensuring that each death is reported by at least one responsible person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To answer Mr Derrick Goh's query on overseas deaths, yes, the RG may register the overseas death of a Singapore Citizen or Permanent Resident under clause 28 if the death is not registered overseas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is provided that the body of the deceased person is brought to Singapore and an application is made by a relative of the deceased person within three months of the death, accompanied by a document issued by a medical practitioner that certifies the cause of death and other death particulars of the deceased person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Gan asked about death registration for missing persons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The next-of-kin of a missing person who wishes to have the missing person presumed by law to be dead will need to apply to the Court for the necessary order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This process is governed by the Evidence Act and will remain so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Once the next-of-kin obtains the Court order, they can inform ICA to update the person's status in its system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This information will be shared with other agencies to facilitate other post-death matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: ICA will also issue a letter of acknowledgement to the next-of-kin when they report the presumption of death to ICA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In the past five years, ICA encountered an average of five reports per year in relation to such Court orders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about newborn children whose births are not registered by the child's parents or who have been abandoned by their parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This makes up less than 0.2% of total births in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Out of these 72 births, most parents do come forward to register the births after reminders from ICA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Due to ICA's efforts to trace the parents, the number of cases of parents who fail to register their child's birth is very low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nevertheless, the Bill will provide powers for the RG to register such births on his own volition when the parents fail to do so despite ICA's efforts to contact and remind them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As for abandoned babies, such cases are relatively rare in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: MSF's Child Protection Service will initially place the abandoned baby under its foster care service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Depending on the circumstances of the case, the child may subsequently be returned to the parents or be put up for adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how ICA will follow up with the responsible persons for a child in cases with incomplete birth particulars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: ICA will do its part to contact and remind the responsible persons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: But, ultimately, it is the responsibility of the responsible persons, such as parents, to register their child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the naming of a child whose birth is registered by the RG on his own volition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The RG will give the child an identifier which will be a single-worded name.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The responsible persons for the child can subsequently apply to the RG to replace the identifier with another name within seven years of the child's birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The responsible persons can, of course, do so much earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked whether birth registration and citizenship will continue to be independent of each other.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: All births in Singapore have to be reported and registered, regardless of the nationalities of the child's parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, the policy remains that a birth that is registered in Singapore does not automatically confer Singapore Citizenship on the child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There is also a small number of children born to at least one Singaporean parent but are not granted Singapore Citizenship for reasons such as the parents not being legally married at the time of the child's birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about children who are stateless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To clarify, children are only classified as stateless when their parents fail to obtain citizenship – Singapore or otherwise – for the child after the child's birth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: A child is not classified as stateless at the time of the birth, nor at the point of the birth registration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It is the responsibility of the parents to obtain the appropriate citizenship for their child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: ICA does not keep track of the citizenship status of non-citizen children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about children born to single unwed mothers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Due to privacy reasons, ICA does not specifically share information of such births with MSF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For surnames, we can have double-barrelled surnames of different races.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On what kinds of surnames are not allowed, we follow the same guidelines as for names.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, as long as names are not offensive like "Stupid" or "Satan", then it will be alright.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We are very mindful of that because we want to protect the dignity of the child.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This change can be done online for those that were previously registered with a single-barrelled race.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On the suggestion on having more ethnic characters or multiple types of ethnic characters, it is something that we can look into.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, as you know, there are some constraints that we have to take into consideration like space availability on the NRIC and the birth certificate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Member also asked about whether we have engaged the undertakers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Essentially, we have been working very closely with the stakeholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It is not only about engaging them, we receive feedback from the different stakeholders at different points in time, including from the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we will continue to engage them even after the Bill is passed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Essentially, it is a continuous engagement and we are mindful that this is about birth and death, which are very sensitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We want to give as much convenience as possible to the families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We often receive feedback from the public and the undertakers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will continue to engage all these stakeholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Member raised issues relating to potential delays by medical practitioners certifying death at home under the new death registration process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Essentially, the medical practitioner will be using the same online system as today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have not heard  much of an issue about delay, so we feel that it will be business as usual.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nevertheless, we will continue to keep a look-out to see if there is any delay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Member also raised issues relating to the abuse of NRICs of the deceased.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For now, we do not see that as a big issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In fact, we have high penalties for this, and I think that in itself is a deterrent for people who want to use this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Member also asked for data and trends of mixed parentage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I do not have the data on hand now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Member may want to submit a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Member also asked about those who are non-digitally savvy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The relatives of the deceased may request the hospital or medical practitioner to help to print out a copy of the digital death certificate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nevertheless, we will take note of this feedback.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: At the end of the day, we want to make sure that everyone enjoys convenience as a result of this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In fact, when the Bill was first read, I received a lot of positive feedback from some of the stakeholders who are very involved in such an area.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They shared with me that it is very much welcomed, especially for the death registration, as they find that it is something that will make it easier and will enhance the process of preparing for the post-death matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We want to make it convenient for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Birth is a celebration, and now, like what the Member shared earlier, it is about having all the different parentage, and I think it is about how we can continue to make ourselves relevant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I also want to cover an area raised by Mr Zhulkarnain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He asked whether ICA will be forming a new department to undertake the enforcement of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Therefore, ICA will not need to form a new department.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: (In Malay):   This Bill will streamline and digitalise the birth, death and stillbirth reporting and registration processes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This will provide significantly greater convenience for the public, in particular, for deaths, when a person passes away, a medical practitioner will examine the body and certify the cause of death online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The death particulars are sent electronically to the Registrar-General of Births and Deaths, who will automatically register the death.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The relatives of the deceased person no longer need to register the death at the hospital, a Neighbourhood Police Centre or Post, or ICA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The relative may then download the digital death certificate from the My Legacy website.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Members asked whether there will be any extra charges or costs to be borne under the streamlined death registration process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While the Government is not able to dictate the fees charged by private hospitals and general practitioners who make house visits to certify deaths, we note that private hospitals and general practitioners will continue to use the same ICA e-service which they currently already use to certify deaths online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Hence, we do not expect the costs incurred by private hospitals and general practitioners to increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, in conclusion, I am confident that this Bill will provide greater convenience for Singaporeans when dealing with births, deaths and stillbirths.
